title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis
subtitle: Right drug, right time, stop at the end

sources.title: Global guidelines for the prevention of surgical site infection (first edition 2016, second edition 2018)
Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis in surgery

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment (NG125)
Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use in Common Syndromes

red_flags.text: Prophylaxis continued for days 'to be safe' after a clean or clean-contaminated operation. It adds resistance, Clostridioides difficile and kidney injury, not protection.
A dose given on the ward hours before transfer to theatre, or after the incision: mistimed prophylaxis is close to no prophylaxis.
A contaminated or dirty operation labelled as 'prophylaxis': that patient needs treatment, with a defined course.
A penicillin allergy label accepted without asking what happened. Most labels are not true IgE-mediated allergy, and avoiding a beta-lactam increases infection risk.
Known MRSA carriage, which changes the agent.

do_now.text: Give prophylaxis as a single intravenous dose before incision. ASHP/IDSA/SIS/SHEA advise starting within 60 minutes before incision (120 minutes for vancomycin and fluoroquinolones); WHO advises within 120 minutes, taking the drug's half-life into account.
Confirm at the time out that prophylaxis has been given and when.

Choose a narrow agent that covers the likely organisms of the operative site, usually a first-generation cephalosporin such as cefazolin, with anaerobic cover added for colorectal and some other operations, per the local or ICMR policy.
Dose by weight: cefazolin 2 g for adults, 3 g for those weighing 120 kg or more, per ASHP/IDSA/SIS/SHEA.

assess.text: Classify the wound: clean (no viscus entered), clean-contaminated (controlled entry into the respiratory, alimentary or genitourinary tract), contaminated (spillage, open fresh trauma, acute non-purulent inflammation), dirty (pus, perforated viscus, old trauma).

Prophylaxis is indicated for clean-contaminated operations, for clean operations with an implant or prosthesis, and where infection would be catastrophic. For other clean operations, follow the procedure-specific recommendation, because the evidence differs between procedures.
Take an allergy history that describes the reaction. A remote non-severe rash is not a contraindication to cefazolin in most patients; anaphylaxis or a severe cutaneous reaction is.
Renal function for agents whose redosing interval changes, and MRSA status where screening exists.

investigate.text: MRSA screening where local policy requires it before implant surgery.
Allergy delabelling pathways, where available, for patients with a low-risk penicillin allergy history.

resuscitate.text: Redose intraoperatively when the operation exceeds two half-lives of the agent (around every 4 hours for cefazolin) or blood loss exceeds 1500 mL in adults.
Supporting measures: clip rather than shave hair if removal is needed, alcohol-based chlorhexidine skin preparation, and normothermia.
Decolonise known Staphylococcus aureus nasal carriers with mupirocin and chlorhexidine before cardiothoracic and orthopaedic surgery.

definitive.text: Stop prophylaxis at the end of the operation. WHO recommends against continuing it after the operation to prevent surgical site infection.
Do not continue prophylaxis because a drain or line is in place.
Contaminated and dirty operations receive treatment-course antibiotics, kept short and defined after source control.
For true beta-lactam allergy, use the locally recommended alternative, typically clindamycin or vancomycin, with Gram-negative cover added when the operation requires it.
Follow the hospital antibiotic policy, which reflects local resistance patterns, and audit compliance.

escalate.text: Microbiology or infectious diseases for MRSA carriers, multidrug-resistant colonisation, and complex allergy.
Antimicrobial stewardship team for audit of timing, choice and duration.
Allergy service for patients whose label blocks first-line agents repeatedly.

notes: Prophylaxis protects the wound during the operation. Its benefit is in tissue concentration at the moment of contamination, which is why timing matters more than duration.
Prolonged post-operative prophylaxis is one of the commonest forms of antibiotic misuse in Indian and international hospitals and is a target of every stewardship programme.
A good time out question is not 'antibiotics given?' but 'what was given, and at what time?'.
